overview: Two patterns of inheritance for traits carried on autosomes, differing in how many copies of the allele are needed to show the trait.
genZNote: Dominant: one bad copy is enough to cause trouble. Recessive: needs both parents to unknowingly team up.

aspects.label: Copies Needed to Express
aspects.valueA: One copy of the mutant allele is enough to show the trait (heterozygotes are affected).
aspects.valueB: Two copies of the mutant allele are needed (only homozygotes are affected).

aspects.label: Unaffected Carrier Parents Possible?
aspects.valueA: Rare — carriers without the allele don't exist; if you have the allele, you usually show the trait.
aspects.valueB: Common — heterozygous carriers appear completely normal.

aspects.label: Example
aspects.valueB: Cystic fibrosis, sickle cell anaemia, phenylketonuria.

aspects.label: Can It Skip a Generation?
aspects.valueA: Rarely skips a generation if penetrance is complete.
aspects.valueB: Can appear to 'skip' generations, resurfacing when two carriers have children.

overlay.examHighYieldNote: Two unaffected (carrier) parents having an affected child is the classic pedigree clue for autosomal recessive inheritance.
overlay.memoryTrick: Dominant = loud, shows every generation. Recessive = quiet, can hide in carriers.
overlay.commonMisconception: An autosomal dominant disease is not necessarily more common than a recessive one — commonness and dominance are separate ideas.
